name: U.S. Department of Education: AI Guidance and Use-Case Inventory
title: U.S. Department of Education: AI Guidance and Use-Case Inventory
answer: This U.S. Department of Education page describes federal AI guidance, innovation and risk management, and presents an inventory of the Department's AI use-cases. Its most useful content is that inventory: named tools such as CAISY, Grammarly, Otter.AI and AWS Bedrock, plus generic uses like summarization, code generation, mock data and outreach drafting. It states that OCIO supports adherence to federal AI regulations and responsible, secure AI use under an executive order. It does not provide detailed school-facing rules, procurement steps or dates.

sections.body: The U.S. Department of Education publishes this page. It is a federal AI guidance landing page that points to an inventory of the Department's AI use-cases. It covers AI guidance, innovation and risk management, and says OCIO supports adherence to federal AI regulations and responsible, secure AI use in line with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The harvested text states no publication or update date. It does not present itself as school-specific policy or procurement guidance.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says it offers information on federal AI guidance, innovation and risk management, and an inventory of the Department of Education's AI use-cases. It states that OCIO supports the Department's adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and responsible, secure AI use while embracing innovative technologies, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The inventory describes named tools and general uses. CAISY is described as enhancing decision-making and operational efficiency through real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation. Grammarly's AI assistant is described as improving written communication with real-time feedback, suggestions and language refinement. Otter.AI is described as providing real-time transcription and collaboration for meetings, interviews, lectures and other audio, creating searchable transcripts and improving accessibility. AWS Bedrock is described as enabling organizations to build and scale applications powered by foundation models for text generation, summarization, conversational AI, personalization and content creation. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines, code snippets in various languages, R code for data analysis, mock data sets, and sample code for syntax and troubleshooting. AI is also listed for extracting key points and action items from public documents, converting data types such as county names to FIPS codes, training employees on prompt engineering, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, suggesting public position descriptions and workflow diagrams, and crafting messages by analyzing tone, structure and relevance. It also says AI is given fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives no specific numbers, dates or formal definitions. It does give positions: OCIO supports adherence to federal AI regulations and responsible, secure AI use under the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; the Department has assembled an inventory of AI use-cases; and it names CAISY, Grammarly, Otter.AI and AWS Bedrock among the tools described.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Education can use this page as a federal source for how the U.S. Department of Education describes its own AI activity and oversight. It shows the kinds of AI uses a federal education agency lists, including transcription for lectures, writing assistance, summarization, code generation, data conversion and mock data. It also signals the compliance frame, federal regulations, responsible and secure use, and an executive order. However, the harvested text does not contain school-facing rules on permissible use, risk or procurement, so it is more useful as an inventory and orientation page than as detailed guidance for schools.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The text is a short landing page and inventory, not a full policy document. It does not state a publication or update date. It does not set out school-specific permissible use, risk-management procedures or procurement requirements. It names third-party tools such as Grammarly, Otter.AI and AWS Bedrock, so parts read as product descriptions. The harvested text is partial and does not include the linked guidance itself.
